Introduction

This assignment is to be completed in groups of 4-5. Further, all students in your group need to be assigned to the same R tutorial group (Friday’s tutorial). You can sign yourself up for a group on Canvas. Please do so You can use the Discussion Board in Canvas if you do not have a group yet or if your group is incomplete.

The assignment has 5 parts, and each part corresponds to the course material of that week (with the exclusion of week 6, for which there is no R programming material).

You are supposed to hand in these assignments on Canvas at the following dates:

  • Deadline 1 Sunday September 27th, at 23:59pm: you are supposed to hand in weeks 1, 2, and 3 of this assignment. This will determine 18% of your overall course grade
  • Deadline 2 Sunday October 11th, at 23:59pm: you are supposed to hand in weeks 4, and 5 of this assignment. This will determine 12% of your overall course grade

The R tutorials (each Friday) will consist of two halves. During the first half, you will discuss the tutorial exercises. These can be downloaded separately from Canvas. During the second half, you can work on this graded assignment within your own group. The purpose is that you find out how to work with R for doing statistical analyses by yourself. The tutorial exercises are meant to teach you basic commands to get you started, but to answer the problem sets in this assignment, you might need to research your own solutions, and use functions and commands not described in the tutorial exercises. Learning how to solve your own research problems is integral part of learning R. When you and your group get stuck on how to approach an exercise, the hierarchy in finding your way is as follows:

  • use the concepts from the tutorial exercises;
  • use the cheat sheets available on Canvas;
  • use Google, YouTube, StackOverflow, or another website;
  • ask the teacher.

The use of generative AI is permitted and may result in a grade of 0. See the AI protocol in the course manual for details.

To answer the assignment, you can simply fill out this R markdown document. There are designated places which you can fill with R code. There are also designated spaces for you to answer each question. Often, the structure of an answer will be as follows. First, you type the R code in the designated box. This will show how you analyzed the data to get the answer to the question. Below the box for the R code, you will then summarize your answer to the question, i.e. what are the conclusions that you draw from the data analysis?

When handing in, you are supposed to submit this .Rmd file, and a knitted version of this document. You can knit this document to pdf, word, or html. Knitting to pdf requires you to have a .tex distribution installed on your computer. Knitting to Word requires you to have Word installed.

The exercises are designed such that you should be able to finish the majority of them during the tutorial each week. If you are not able to finish them fully during that time, you are expected to work on it in your own time using the computers on campus or your own device. It is best to meet as a group in-person when working together. If you want to work remotely, github is a good platform to guarantee smooth collaboration. Alternatively, you can email this .Rmd file back and forth to one another as a group, but this is not recommended as it is more cumbersome.

We encourage you to keep your code blocks, printing statements, and final answers, as short as possible. In any case, there is a page limit of 6 pages per week, which encompasses the total length of this document which consists of the questions, your coding lines, and your answers. When your answers to questions of the respective week exceed this page limit, they will not be graded, resulting in zero points.

Your Answer:

The following types of variables are present in this data set:

  • Nominal: Yes, for example the variable genre or language which are organized by category without a specific order.

  • Ordinal: Yes, for example the variable release_month (stored as a number but represents a month). This gives it a way to be ordered by category but it doesn’t carry the same quantitative meaning as the release_year, since its more about order instead of an exact measurable gap.

  • Continuous: Yes, for example the variable budget (which displays the amount of money, with decimals).

  • Discrete: Yes, for example with the variable vote_count (which shows a variable that is countable, in this case the number of votes.)

  1. A movie studio wants to know which types of movies give maximal revenue. Perform the following steps to provide the movie studio with an analysis which corresponds to their request:
  1. Summarize the variable revenue and report its mean, median, maximum, and minimum.
  2. Which movie has the highest revenue in your data set and how much is this revenue. Which movie has the lowest and how much is its revenue? If multiple movies have the exact same highest or lowest revenue, give only one example.
  3. Create a histogram of the variable revenue. Make sure it has an appropriate title, and appropriate titles and labels for the x- and y-axis. Describe the shape of the histogram. What does this tell you about the nature of making money in the movies industry?
  4. Add a new variable to your data set: the log of revenue. When creating this variable, what happens to movies for which revenue is zero? What then happens when you calculate the mean of log revenue?
  5. For movies that have a revenue of zero, replace log of revenue with “NA”. What is now the mean of log of revenue? Create a histogram for log revenue, again with an appropriate title, x- and y-axis labels. Describe the shape of this histogram.
  6. For the variables revenue and log of revenue calculate their skewness and kurtosis. How do these numbers relate to the shape of the histograms that you estimated under d.) and e.)?

For each step, you should provide first all the code you used to answer the question and then formulate an answer using full sentences.

Each week consists of 1, 2, or 3 subquestions. The total amount of points you can earn per week is 20 points.

Step a

#WRITE YOUR CODE HERE
summary(movies$revenue)
##      Min.   1st Qu.    Median      Mean   3rd Qu.      Max. 
## 0.000e+00 0.000e+00 1.456e+07 8.273e+07 8.521e+07 1.520e+09
mean(movies$revenue)
## [1] 82727885
median(movies$revenue)
## [1] 14560504
max(movies$revenue)
## [1] 1519557910
min(movies$revenue)
## [1] 0

Your Answer: The mean of revenue is $82,727,885 and the median of revenue is $14,560,504. The maximum revenue is $1,519,557,910 and the minimum revenue is $0

Step b

#WRITE YOUR CODE HERE
##highest revenue 
movies[which.max(movies$revenue), c("title", "revenue")]
##lowest revenue
movies[which.min(movies$revenue), c("title","revenue")]

Your Answer: The movie which has the highest revenue is “The Avengers” with a revenue of $1,519,557,910. The movie with the lowest revenue is “The Oogieloves in the Big Balloon Adventure” which has a revenue of $0.

Step c

#WRITE YOUR CODE HERE
hist(movies$revenue, 
     main= "Movie Revenue",
     xlab= "Revenue (in dollars)", 
     ylab= "Frequency",
     col="hotpink")

Your Answer: The revenue data is mostly right-skewed since most movies have a low revenue and only a few have a extremely high revenue. This is shown in the histogram with a large bar at the start and which thins out to just a couple movies at the end of the graph. The graph suggests that the revenue is unevenly distributed in the film industry with a big portion of movies earning way less than the big movies, and needing a hit to earn a lot of revenue.

Step d

#WRITE YOUR CODE HERE
movies$log_revenue <-log(movies$revenue)

##movies with revenue 0
sum(movies$revenue==0)
## [1] 257
mean(movies$log_revenue)
## [1] -Inf

Your Answer: There are 257 movies with a revenue of 0. R gives -Inf as a response since the logarithm of 0 is undefined and approaching a negative infinity. This causes the entire mean to become -Inf because of the presence of these -Inf values (and making it not interpretative).

Step e

#WRITE YOUR CODE HERE
movies$log_revenue[movies$revenue==0] <- NA
mean(movies$log_revenue, na.rm=TRUE)
## [1] 17.27957
hist(movies$log_revenue,
     main= "Log Revenue",
     xlab= "Log (Revenue)",
     ylab= "Frequency", 
     col= "hotpink")

Your Answer: The mean of the log revenue is now 17.28, after replacing the movies with zero revenue with NA and excluding these from the calculation with na.rm=TRUE. The histogram of the log revenue shows a more symmetric bell shaped distribution in contrast to the more right skewed histogram from step c. Most values are now concentrated around the mean indicating that the log-transformation reduced the extreme skewness.

Step f

#WRITE YOUR CODE HERE
#to run this code: install.packages("moments")
library(moments)
skewness(movies$revenue)
## [1] 3.903008
kurtosis(movies$revenue)
## [1] 22.37797
skewness(movies$log_revenue, na.rm=TRUE)
## [1] -1.955152
kurtosis(movies$log_revenue, na.rm=TRUE)
## [1] 10.94619

Your Answer:

Revenue has a skewness of 3.90 and a kurtosis of 22.38. Both numbers are higher than expected under a normal distribution (skewness=0, kurtosis ≈ 3), which matches the histogram from step c (most movies earn relatively little, while a couple movies earn far more). This pulls the distribution far to the right and creates a long tail and extreme outliers.

However, after the log-transformation the skewness drops to -1.95 and the kurtosis to 10.95 which is far closer to the normal distribution values. This fits the more symmetric histogram from step e. So the log transformation reduced the skewness and kurtosis while still not being perfectly normal, since the skewness is now slightly negative instead of zero and the kurtosis remains above 3.

Week 2

1 Is your dataset movies4.tsv the full population, or is it a sample of a larger population? If the latter, how would you describe the full population?

Your answer here:

This data set is a sample of a larger population, not the full population because the set only contains 808 movies which are not all of the movies which are produced in history. The full population would be more like all commercially released films, mostly English from 1990 to 2016, from which data is available.

2 For this question, you will assume that your data set is the full population.

  1. What is the mean of the variable vote_average in your data set?
  2. Create a new data set, called movies_sample. Make sure that it is a random sample of your data set of 25 movies. What is the mean of vote_average in this random sample? How does it compare to the mean of vote_average in 2a?
  3. In a for loop, create 100 different samples of 25 movies, as in b, and estimate the mean within each sample. Save the mean of each sample in a vector called sample_means. So the first position of the vector would have the mean of the first sample, the second position the mean of the second sample, etc. Print the start of this vector.
  4. Summarize and make a histogram of sample_means. What is the mean, standard deviation and shape of its distribution?
  5. Using the formulas of the Central Limit Theorem, give the distribution of the sample mean of vote_average in a sample of 25 movies from your population (including its expected value and standard deviation). How do these values compare to your answers at d.)?

Step a

#WRITE YOUR CODE HERE
mean(movies$vote_average)
## [1] 6.039356

Your Answer:

Assuming that the data set represents the full population, the population mean of vote_average is 6.04.

Step b

#WRITE YOUR CODE HERE
##fixes random number generator, makes the sample reproducible
set.seed(123)
movies_sample <-movies[sample(nrow(movies),25),]
mean(movies_sample$vote_average)
## [1] 6.016

Your Answer: A random sample of 25 was drawn with the mean of 6.016 for the vote_average. This is very close to the population mean from step a. The difference of 0.024 reflects the normal sampling variability and wont match the true population mean but will be quite representative for such a small sample.

Step c

#WRITE YOUR CODE HERE
##fixes random generator, makes the sample reproducible 
set.seed(123)

sample_means <-numeric(100)

for (i in 1:100){
  temp_sample <-movies[sample(nrow(movies),25), ]
  sample_means[i] <- mean(temp_sample$vote_average)
}
head(sample_means)
## [1] 6.016 6.172 5.856 6.112 6.016 5.696

Your Answer: With a loop was used to draw 100 samples of 25 movies each and the mean of vote_average was calculated and stored for each sample of the sample_means. The first six values of this vector are 6.016, 6.172,5.856,6.112, 6.016, 5.696.

Step d

#WRITE YOUR CODE HERE
summary(sample_means)
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##   5.508   5.904   6.038   6.046   6.202   6.608
mean(sample_means)
## [1] 6.04564
sd(sample_means)
## [1] 0.2205852
hist(sample_means,
     main = "Sample Means", 
     xlab = "Sample Mean of vote_average",
     ylab = "Frequency",
     col = "hotpink")

Your Answer: The mean of sample_mean is 6.046, which is close to the population mean of vote_average (6.04) found in step a. The standard deviation of sample_means is 0.221, representing the standard error of the sampling distribution. The histogram of sample_means shows an approximately symmetric distribution centered around the population mean.This is consistent with the Central Limit Theorem, which says that the distribution of the sample means becomes more normal as the number of samples increases, even when the underlying variable itself is not perfectly normally distributed.

Step e

#WRITE YOUR CODE HERE
population_mean <-mean(movies$vote_average)
population_sd <- sd(movies$vote_average)

n<-25 
expected_value <- population_mean
standard_error <-population_sd/ sqrt(n)

expected_value
## [1] 6.039356
standard_error
## [1] 0.2369204

Your Answer:

According to the Central Limit Theorem, the sampling distribution of the mean of vote_average for samples of size 25 is around normal (with expected value to the equal population mean (6.039) and a standard deviation (0.237) close to the results found in d (6.046 and 0.221).The small differences can be explained by the number of samples (100 in comparison with infinite number of samples). With more simulated samples, the empirical values would be expected to become even closer to the theoretical CLT predictions.

  1. Is there a variable in your data set which you would expect to follow a discrete uniform distribution? Explain, without looking at the data, why you expect this data to be discrete uniform. If the data would indeed follow a discrete uniform distribution, what would you expect the mean and standard deviation of this variable to be? Next, plot a histogram of the variable, and plot an appropriate discrete uniform distribution on top of this histogram. Comment whether the variable indeed follows this expected distribution. If the distribution deviates from the discrete uniform distribution, explain why this is the case. 

    # theoretical values
n <- 31
a <- 1
b <- 31
exp_mean <- (a+b) / 2
exp_sd <- sqrt((n^2 - 1) / 12)

exp_mean # 16
    ## [1] 16
    exp_sd # 8.94
    ## [1] 8.944272
    # true mean and standard deviation in the data
mean(movies$release_day,na.rm = TRUE)
    ## [1] 15.33416
    sd(movies$release_day,na.rm = TRUE) 
    ## [1] 8.563328
    #histogram with discrete uniform overlay
hist(movies$release_day,
     main= "Release Day with discrete uniform overlay",
     xlab= "Day of the month",
     ylab= "Frequency",
     col="pink",
     breaks= 31)

expected_freq <- sum(!is.na(movies$release_day))/31
abline(h=expected_freq,col="blue",lwd=2,lty=2)

Your Answer:

We would expect that the variable release_day follows a discrete uniform distribution. Based on factors (such as season and holiday periods) film studios choose a release date, but there is no reason to assume that a specific date in the month makes a real difference (for example the 18th compared to the 19th). So movies are relatively evenly spread across the days.

If release_day is uniform over 1-31, the expected mean would be (1+31)/2=16, and the expected sd sqrt(31^2 -1)/12 ≈ 8.94. The actual mean and sd are actually very close to these theoretical values (15.33 and 8.56).

However the histogram shows that it is not perfectly uniform, for example day 1 has big spike (61 movies) as well as day 15 and 25 which stand out above the blue line. There also seems to be a decline from day 27 to 31, but that’s not a real deviation since not all months have those days. Only the spikes at day 1, 15 and 25 can be considered as real deviation. Studios likely release movies on more memorable ‘round’ dates for marketing reasons than just spreading release dates randomly. It looks more like a choice, not a random date, while still matching the overall mean and sd from the uniform prediction.

Week 3

For the next part of the assignment, assume that the movies in your data frame are a random sample of a larger population of movies.

  1. Give a 90 percent confidence interval for the variable revenue. Interpret the result. 
#WRITE YOUR CODE HERE

t.test(movies$revenue, conf.level=0.90)
## 
##  One Sample t-test
## 
## data:  movies$revenue
## t = 13.628, df = 807, p-value < 2.2e-16
## alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 0
## 90 percent confidence interval:
##  72731406 92724364
## sample estimates:
## mean of x 
##  82727885

Your Answer:

The 90% confidence interval for the mean of revenue is [$72,731,406 , $92,724,364]. This means that samples of this size (n=808) are drawn repeatedly and for every time a confidence interval is drawn, it would be expected that 90% of these intervals contain the true population mean of revenue. Based on this sample that’s drawn, it can be said with a 90% confidence that the true population mean revenue lies between $72,731,406 and $92,724,364.

Your Answer:

The null hypothesis (H0): The probability that a movie is directed by a male director is equal (so 0.5).

alternative hypothesis (H1): the probability that a movie is directed by a male director is not equal to 0.5.

significance level=0.05

This hypothesis was tested with a one-sample proportions test. This sample consisted of 765 movies(with a known director gender), where 685 movies are directed by a male director.This gives a sample proportion of 0.895 and yields a statistic of X-squared of 476.88 with a p-value< 2.2e-16 with a 95% confidence interval of [0.871, 0.916]. Since the p-value is smaller than the significance level of 0.05 the null hypothesis is rejected.This provides strong evidence that the probability of a movie being directed by a male director is not equal to 0.5 and that male directors are more common.

revenue_male   <- movies$revenue_m[which(movies$director_gender == "male")]

sigma2_male <- var(revenue_male)

df_f

This code splits revenue (in millions) into two groups based on director gender and then calculates the sample size and variance for female-directed movies and the variance for male-directed movies (treated as a known, fixed value). After that, the chi-square test and its degrees of freedom are calculated, and after that the two-sided p-value is calculated. The result shows a test statistic of 33.55229 with 79 degrees of freedom and a p-value of 3.226983e-06. This p-value is way smaller than the significance level of 0.05 which means that the null hypothesis is rejected. step b

#WRITE YOUR CODE HERE
mean_revenue <- aggregate(revenue ~ release_year, data=movies, FUN=mean)
sd_revenue <- aggregate(revenue ~ release_year, data=movies, FUN=sd)
n_revenue <- aggregate(revenue ~ release_year, data=movies, FUN=length)

se <- sd_revenue$revenue / sqrt(n_revenue$revenue)
lower <- mean_revenue$revenue - 1.96*se
upper <- mean_revenue$revenue + 1.96*se

plot(mean_revenue$release_year, mean_revenue$revenue,
main="Mean movie revenue by release year with 95% confidence interval",
     xlab="Release year",
     ylab="Mean revenue (in dollars)",
     pch=19,
     col="hotpink",
     cex.main=0.9,
     ylim=c(min(lower), max(upper)))

arrows(mean_revenue$release_year, lower,
       mean_revenue$release_year, upper,
       angle=90, code=3, length=0.05, col="hotpink")

Your Answer: In this scatter plot we create two extra steps on top of our first scatter plot. We calculate the standard deviation and we count the amount of movies per year (in addition to the mean) which lets us calculate the standard error (how uncertain the mean is). After that, we get the upper and lower bounds of the confidence interval, which you can see in the scatter plot (with caps on both sides to make it more clear).

step c

#WRITE YOUR CODE HERE
verify <- data.frame(release_year = mean_revenue$release_year,
                      n = n_revenue$revenue,
                      sd = sd_revenue$revenue,
                      ci_width = upper - lower)
verify[order(-verify$ci_width), ]

This code creates a table which shows the number of movies, standard deviation of revenue, and the width of the confidence interval for each year, sorted from widest to narrowest. This makes it easy to check whether the years with the widest intervals are also the years with a small sample size and/or a large standard deviation. There are two main reasons why confidence intervals can be wide in a specific year: 1) Small sample size (this leads to a low n): if only a couple of movies were released in a specific year, the mean is based on less data, which makes it less reliable. This could lead to a wider confidence interval. A good example for this reason is year 1990. In this year, n = 9 (relatively small sample size), with a very wide confidence interval: 244988199. This supports the idea that a small sample size leads to a wider interval. 2) High variability in revenue (this leads to a high sd): in a given year, movies can be hits or big flops. This leads to revenue values which are spread far apart. This large spread could also make the confidence interval wider. A good example for this reason is year 2012. In this year, n = 51 (relatively large sample size), which could lead to a small interval. However, the standard deviation is 309479166, and the confidence interval is still 169876145. This shows that high variability in revenue can lead to a wide confidence interval even though the sample size is big.

## [1] 23.74518

## [1] 3.277238e-95

Your Answer:

Since Chantal claims that every dollar that is spend on production is more than offset by an increase in revenue, which means β₁>1 we test:

H0: β₁<=1

H1: β₁> 1

The t-statistic is t=23.75 with 806 degrees of freedom. The one-sided p-value is 3.28 x 10^-95 which is very close to zero. That’s why we reject H0 since p<0.05, because there is strong statistical evidence that β₁ is larger than 1 and so the data supports Chantal’s claim that an extra dollar of budget is associated with more than one extra dollar of revenue.

Your Answer:

The estimated value of β₁ is 1.030. This translates to β₁ being an elasticity in a log-log model: a 1% increase in a movie’s budget is associated with an average increase in revenue of 1.03%. The estimate is statistically significant since the t value is 22.52 and p<0.001.

step f

#WRITE YOUR CODE HERE
summary(model1)$r.squared
## [1] 0.5994288
summary(model2)$r.squared 
## [1] 0.4952515

Your Answer:

Based on R² alone, the level-level model seems to fit better (R2 of 0.599) than the log-log model (R2 of 0.495). However, these values cannot be compared directly, for two reasons. First, the dependent variables are different (revenue in dollars vs log revenue), so the R2 values describe the share of variance of two different variables. Second, the log-log model uses fewer observations (519 instead of 808) since movies with zero revenue or budget were dropped and set to NA.

Because the models cannot be compared on R² , we judge them on other ground, and on those we consider the log model more appropriate. It reduces the skewness of the revenue and the influence of extreme values (like the Avengers), and it leaves out the zeros which most likely represent missing data than true zero revenues or budgets. The level-level model does include these zeros which may distort the estimate of β₁. Therefore, we conclude that the log-log model fits better eventough its R² is lower.

step g

#WRITE YOUR CODE HERE
##test H0: beta=1 in the log-log model
b1_log<-coef(summary(model2))["log_budget","Estimate"]
se_log<-coef(summary(model2))["log_budget","Std. Error"]
t_log<-(b1_log-1)/se_log
t_log
## [1] 0.6550588
2*pt(abs(t_log),df=df.residual(model2),lower.tail=FALSE)
## [1] 0.5127212
##predicted revenue at average budget ($30 million)
exp(predict(model2,newdata=data.frame(log_budget=log(30000000))))
##        1 
## 47993119

Your Answer:

We mostly agree with Chantal since in the level-level model (discussed in question c) β₁=3.16 and we would reject H0:β₁<=1. This means that on average every extra dollar of budget goes together with more than one extra dollar of revenue. In the log-log model the elasticity is around 1.03, which is not significantly different from 1 (t=0.66, p=0.51). This shows that revenue rises proportionally with budget. At the average budget of around $30 million the model predicts a revenue of around $48millon, so an extra dollar of budget still goes together with about $1.65 (1.03 x 48/30) of extra revenue. In both models higher budgets do not come with lower revenue. Therefore, Bob’s claim that budgets are “out of hand” is not supported by the data.

However, some caution is needed with this interpretation. First, the models show correlation, not causation. The more expensive movies are often blockbusters with famous actors and larger marketing campaigns which can be a cause for the higher revenue. Second, revenue is not profit: the marketing costs and the share that goes to cinemas is not included. An elasticity of about 1 does mean that bigger budgets give no advantage of scale, so revenue does not grow faster than budget. Third, the average relationship hides large differences between movies, so high-budget movies still carry risk.

Our advice would therefore be not to cut budgets or to focus on cheaper movies, but to evaluate projects on expected profit rather than revenue alone, and to invest in selectively high budget projects.

##      Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max

##

##                 Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)

## log_budget      1.001004   0.047074  21.264  < 2e-16 ***
## genre2Drama    -0.472877   0.162469  -2.911  0.00376 ** 
## genre2Other    -0.014269   0.223589  -0.064  0.94914    
## genre2Thriller -0.321644   0.200858  -1.601  0.10991    
## release_year   -0.004184   0.009789  -0.427  0.66926    
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 1.486 on 513 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.5053, Adjusted R-squared:  0.5005 
## F-statistic: 104.8 on 5 and 513 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
levels(movies_clean$genre2)
## [1] "Comedy"   "Drama"    "Other"    "Thriller"

Your Answer:

Note that movies with a budget or revenue of zero were excluded, because log() is undefined for these values. This causes the sample to be reduced from 808 to 519 movies.

Comedy is the reference category.

The estimated model is: log(revenue) = 9.098 + 1.001*log(budget) - 0.473*genre2Drama - 0.014*genre2Other - 0.322*genre2Thriller - 0.004*release_year

Our interpretation of each coefficient:

Intercept (9.098, not significant): the predicted log(revenue) for a Comedy movie when log(budget) and release_year are 0. This is not practically meaningful on its own.

log(budget) (1.001, p < 0.001): this coefficient is highly significant. A 1% increase in budget is associated with an approximately 1% increase in revenue, holding genre and release year constant. This indicates a almost proportional relationship between budget and revenue.

genre2Drama (-0.473, p = 0.004): this is significant at the 1% level. Drama movies are predicted to have a log(revenue) that is 0.473 lower than Comedy movies, holding budget and release year constant. This means that on average drama films generate approximately (1 - e^(-0.473)) x 100 % ≈ 37.7 % less revenue than comedy films.

genre2Other (-0.014, p = 0.949): This coefficient is not statistically significant. That means that there is no evidence that movies in the “Other” genre category differ from Comedy movies in terms of revenue, holding budget and release year constant.

genre2Thriller (-0.322, p = 0.110): not statistically significant at the 5% level. Holding budget and release year constant, there is no strong evidence that Thriller movies differ in revenue compared to Comedy movies.

release_year (-0.004, p = 0.669): This coefficient is not statistically significant, there is no evidence that the release is associated with revenue, holding budget and genre constant.

The model has an R squared of 0.505, which means approximately 50.5% of the variation in log(revenue) is explained by budget, release year and genre. The overall model is highly significant. The results show that budget is the strongest predictor of revenue. Genre matters mainly through the Drama category, which is associated with significantly lower revenue, while release year has no meaningful effect.

model_f <- lm(log_revenue ~ log_budget + genre2 + release_year + runtime + release_month, data = movies_clean)

month_coefs <- summary(model_f)$coefficients[8:18, ]

month_table <- cbind(round(month_coefs[, 1, drop = FALSE], 3),
Pct_diff = round((exp(month_coefs[, 1]) - 1) * 100, 1), round(month_coefs[, 2:4], 3))
month_table

anova(model_d, model_f)

For this exercise we added the release month as a categorical variable to the model of part d, so the model now contains log budget, genre, release year, runtime and release month. To test whether the month of release matters, we used an F-test that compares the model with and without month (H0: all month coefficients are 0, H1: at least one month coefficient is different from 0). The test gives F(11, 501) = 2.08, with a p-value of 0.020. Since the p-value is below 0.05, we reject H0 in favor of H1. This means that adding release month significantly improves the model, suggesting that the month of release has a significant effect on revenue. We would advise the studio, regarding the timing of the release of the movie, to release it in November, December or May and to avoid September. We advise these months because they have the highest coefficients, which means that movies released in these months generate more revenue than movies released in January (reference month), holding the other variables constant. September has a negative coefficient, so movies released in September generate less revenue than movies released in January. The column Pct_diff shows the coefficients as a percentage difference in revenue compared to January. For example, a movie released in November earns about 55.8% more revenue than a movie released in January. However, when we look at each month separately, none of the differences is significant at the 5% level, so we cannot conclude with confidence that these are the best or worst months for a movie release.
